screens.title: Materials and Shaders — the recipe and the chef
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you will see how materials and shaders together produce the look of every visible object in Unity. Think of a material as the recipe that lists color, texture maps, smoothness, and metallic values. A shader is the chef: it reads the recipe, uses scene lighting and camera position, and performs the math on the graphics hardware to produce the final pixel color you see on screen. We will ground this idea in Physically Based Rendering, the modern approach Unity’s Standard Shader uses to make surfaces react plausibly under any lighting. You’ll learn what Albedo, Metallic, Smoothness, Normal maps, Ambient Occlusion, and Emission do, and you’ll see a practical example of a weathered wooden barrel that combines multiple maps to look realistic. Along the way we’ll highlight common mistakes artists make—like treating a material as only a flat color or mixing non-PBR textures with PBR shaders—and cover performance considerations when authoring materials for target hardware. By the end you should be able to explain the relationship between a material and shader, adjust Standard Shader properties with intent, and identify when a texture needs to be authored in a PBR workflow.

screens.title: Material vs Shader
screens.narratorSegment: A material in Unity is a data asset that lists the visual properties of a surface: base color, texture maps, metallic and smoothness values, normal and occlusion maps, and emission settings. It is a collection of values and references to images that describe how the surface should look. A shader is a small program that runs on the graphics hardware and performs per-pixel calculations to combine material properties with lighting and camera information to produce the final visible color. To understand their relationship, imagine making a cake: the material is the recipe listing ingredients and proportions, while the shader is the chef that mixes, heats, and presents the cake. This distinction matters because you can have many materials that use the same shader but with different values; conversely, a shader can be swapped to change how values are interpreted. A common misconception is to call a material a shader. That blurs duties: a material has no execution logic, and a shader without material values has nothing to compute. Example: two plastic toys can share the Standard Shader but differ in Albedo and Smoothness. Misconception check: if a surface appears flat even with a material assigned, verify the shader supports the maps you're using and that your textures were authored for PBR. Key takeaway: treat the material as data and the shader as the program that interprets it.

keyIdea.text: Material = data (recipe). Shader = program (chef). Both are required to render a surface.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Material vs Shader
Core Concept

Material vs Shader

Distinct roles and dependencies you must understand to author predictable surfaces.

Material (data)
Holds Albedo, Metallic, Smoothness, Normal, Occlusion, Emission maps and scalar values.
Shader (program)
Performs lighting and surface math on the GPU to convert material data into pixels.
Quick checklist
  • Materials supply values and textures.
  • Shaders interpret those values using lighting and camera data.
  • Swap shader to change rendering model without changing texture assets.
Example
Two toy models using the Standard Shader with different Albedo and Smoothness values produce distinct looks while the same shader executes rendering code for both.
Misconception
Calling a material a shader hides the difference: one is data, the other is code. They are not interchangeable.
Key Takeaway

Always think in terms of data versus execution: materials describe, shaders compute.

Visual Aid
Recipe analogy

Material lists ingredients like color and maps. Shader follows that list and mixes lighting math to produce the final rendered surface.

Practical check

If a texture has no effect, confirm that the active shader exposes that map slot and that the map is authored for a PBR workflow.

screens.title: What is PBR?
screens.narratorSegment: Physically Based Rendering, or PBR, is a methodology for describing how surfaces interact with light using physically motivated properties. Instead of artist-only tricks for each lighting condition, PBR defines a set of parameters—such as Albedo, Metallic, and Smoothness—that correspond to real-world surface qualities. When you author materials in a PBR workflow, the same material will respond predictably under bright sun, indoor lighting, or colored light sources. That predictability is the main advantage: artists can rely on physical intuition. Concrete example: a metal sphere and a painted plastic sphere with identical Albedo will behave differently if their Metallic and Smoothness values are set correctly; metal will reflect the environment and carry tint, while plastic will scatter light more and show weaker environment reflections. A common misconception is that PBR guarantees photographic realism by default; it does not. PBR guarantees consistent behavior given correct inputs. If textures are authored in a non-PBR pipeline, or metallic maps are incorrect, results will be implausible. Key takeaway: PBR links artist-controlled, physically meaningful parameters to shader calculations so materials remain consistent across scenes and lighting setups.

keyIdea.text: PBR defines materials by physical surface properties so they behave consistently under varied lighting.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › What is PBR?
Definition

Physically Based Rendering (PBR)

A workflow that uses physically meaningful parameters so materials react predictably to lighting.

Core properties
  • Albedo — base color and diffuse reflectance.
  • Metallic — how metallic a surface is; affects reflectance color.
  • Smoothness — determines sharpness of reflections.
  • Normal map — simulates fine surface detail for lighting.
  • Ambient Occlusion — darkens crevices to simulate self-shadowing.
Why it matters
Consistency across environments, clearer artist intent, and reusability of materials.
Example
Set Metallic high and Smoothness high on a sphere to produce a bright, reflective metallic look under environment lighting.
Misconception
PBR is not a shortcut to realism without correct inputs. Textures and maps must be authored for a PBR workflow.
Key Takeaway

Use PBR parameters deliberately. Good inputs plus the Standard Shader produce predictable, physically plausible results.

screens.title: Standard Shader overview
screens.narratorSegment: The Standard Shader in Unity implements a PBR-based rendering model and exposes the key parameters artists use to describe surfaces. At a high level, the shader receives material inputs—Albedo, Metallic, Smoothness, Normal map, Ambient Occlusion, and Emission—and the scene lighting and camera vectors. It first uses Albedo and Metallic to determine diffuse and specular contribution, then applies Smoothness to shape the reflection lobe. Normal maps perturb surface normals so lighting responds to fine detail. Ambient Occlusion multiplies base lighting in crevices to deepen shadows. Emission adds self-illumination that appears to glow regardless of direct lights. A concrete example: the shader may sample Albedo and Metallic maps, compute a fresnel-weighted specular term, blur or sharpen that specular with Smoothness, add normal-based lighting variations, and finally add emission on top. A common misconception is that each slider acts independently; in reality the shader combines them in a formula, so Metallic and Smoothness together determine the character of reflections. Key takeaway: learning how each input participates in the shader’s math helps you predict how changes will appear in scene lighting. Standard Shader overview means standard shader samples material maps, computes diffuse and specular contributions, applies normal perturbation and ao, and adds emission to produce final color.. In practical terms, how the standard shader maps pbr parameters to final pixels. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Shader pipeline
keyIdea.text: Standard Shader samples material maps, computes diffuse and specular contributions, applies normal perturbation and AO, and adds emission to produce final color.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Standard Shader overview
Process Flow

How Standard Shader uses PBR inputs

A step-by-step conceptual pipeline of what the shader calculates from material inputs.

Step 1: Sample maps
Read Albedo, Metallic, Smoothness, Normal, AO, and Emission from the material.
Step 2: Compute diffuse & specular
Combine Albedo and Metallic to partition energy between diffuse and specular reflections.
Step 3: Apply normals & AO
Perturb normals for detail and darken crevices with Ambient Occlusion for depth.
Step 4: Add emission
Emission is added as self-illumination on top of lighting calculations.
Key Takeaway

The shader treats inputs as contributors to physically motivated lighting terms. Adjusting one parameter often changes how others appear.

Compact diagram
Inputs
Albedo · Metallic · Smoothness · Normal · AO · Emission
Shader computation
Sample maps → compute diffuse/specular → shape reflections → apply normals/AO → add emission
Output
Final pixel color that reacts to scene lighting and camera position
Example
High Smoothness narrows reflection highlights; combined with high Metallic this creates the bright, mirror-like appearance of polished metal.

screens.title: Albedo and Texture Maps
screens.narratorSegment: Albedo, Normal, and Ambient Occlusion maps are fundamental texture inputs for PBR materials. Albedo is the base color map that represents diffuse reflectance; it should not contain baked lighting or shadows because the shader expects neutral base color data. A Normal map encodes surface normals to simulate small-scale bumps and detail without extra geometry; it directly affects how light shades a surface, changing highlight placement and silhouette shading. Ambient Occlusion is a multiplier that darkens crevices and areas less exposed to ambient light, enhancing perceived depth. A concrete example: on a wooden barrel, the Albedo would carry the wood grain and color variations, the Normal map would simulate carved plank ridges, and the AO map would darken crevices between planks. Common mistakes include authoring Albedo with strong shadowing baked in, which reduces the shader's ability to respond correctly to scene lighting, or using a diffuse-styled texture meant for non-PBR pipelines. Another pitfall is forgetting to import normal maps with the correct compression or normal map type, which yields flat or incorrect shading. Key takeaway: author textures for PBR—clean Albedo, proper normal map, and AO for subtle self-shadowing—so the shader can combine them correctly.

keyIdea.title: Texture roles
keyIdea.text: Albedo = base color without baked light. Normal = surface detail for lighting. AO = soft self-shadowing multiplier.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Albedo and Texture Maps
Comparison

Albedo · Normal · Ambient Occlusion

Roles and authoring notes for the most common texture inputs in PBR workflows.

Albedo
Base color map. Avoid baked shadows. Provides the diffuse color the shader uses.
Normal map
Encodes surface normals to fake micro-detail. Impacts highlights and shading strongly.
Ambient Occlusion
Darkens crevices to indicate limited ambient light exposure. Multiply with base lighting.
Practical tip
Keep Albedo free of lighting and hue shifts from reflections; let the shader handle lighting response.
Common mistake
Using diffuse textures authored for non-PBR shading will produce inconsistent results with the Standard Shader.
Scenario

Weathered wooden barrel

Albedo provides the grain and color variations. Normal map simulates plank ridges. AO darkens gaps between planks for depth.

Key Takeaway

Author texture maps for PBR: clean Albedo, correctly encoded normals, and AO to boost perceived depth without geometry.

screens.title: Metallic and Smoothness
screens.narratorSegment: Metallic and Smoothness are two of the most impactful properties in the Standard Shader. Metallic controls whether a surface behaves like a conductor—metal—or a dielectric such as plastic or wood. High Metallic causes reflections to carry the surface tint and favor specular energy, while low Metallic leaves color primarily in the diffuse channel. Smoothness controls the microfacet distribution of the surface: high Smoothness produces tight, mirror-like highlights and clear reflections; low Smoothness scatters reflected light, producing a rougher appearance. Together they define the character of reflections. For example, a polished chrome surface will have high Metallic and high Smoothness, making bright, colored reflections; a rough painted metal may have high Metallic but low Smoothness, producing dim and blurred reflections. A common misconception is to treat Smoothness as merely an aesthetic slider; it is a physical parameter that alters light distribution mathematically in the shader. Practical advice: use texture maps for these properties when surfaces vary across the model—like worn edges where metallic paint is scraped away—so the shader computes realistic mixed areas at render time. Key takeaway: adjust Metallic and Smoothness together to model the physical nature of the surface, not to simply make something "shinier."

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Metallic & Smoothness
Core Concept

Metallic and Smoothness

Fundamental controls over reflectivity and the look of highlights on a PBR surface.

Metallic
High values make surfaces act like metal; reflections carry tint and specular dominates.
Smoothness
Controls microfacet roughness. High Smoothness = sharp reflections; low = blurred reflections.
Use maps for wear
Assign Metallic and Smoothness maps to vary reflectivity and roughness across the surface to simulate wear and material transitions.
Example
A scraped metal band on a barrel uses a Metallic map to show metal areas and a Smoothness map to show polished versus rusty rough spots.
Misconception
Do not treat Smoothness as purely decorative; it changes the math that shapes reflection lobes in the shader.
Key Takeaway

Model both the metallicness and micro-surface roughness to achieve believable reflective behavior; use maps for spatial detail.

Visual examples
Polished metal
High Metallic, high Smoothness — mirror-like reflections that pick up environment color.
Rough painted surface
Low Metallic, low Smoothness — diffuse color dominates, reflections are soft and scattered.

screens.title: Normal Maps, Height Maps, and AO
screens.narratorSegment: Normal maps, height maps, and Ambient Occlusion are tools to add surface richness without increasing polygon count. A normal map encodes altered surface normals at the texel level so lighting calculations react as if the surface had micro-geometry. This creates convincing bumps, scratches, or carved details. Height maps (or parallax maps when used) can simulate larger depth shifts by offsetting UVs during shading; they add perceived depth beyond what normal maps provide but can be more expensive. Ambient Occlusion is a grayscale map multiplied into shading to darken crevices where ambient light would be occluded. A practical example: a wooden barrel uses a normal map for plank ridges, a subtle height map to suggest warped planks, and an AO map to deepen the seams between boards. Be careful: importing normal maps properly (flagging them as normal map type) is essential; otherwise the renderer treats them as color textures and shading will be wrong. Misconception check: AO is not a substitute for global illumination; it is a local multiplier to enrich perceived contact shadows. Key takeaway: combine normal, height, and AO maps to increase realism while keeping the base mesh efficient.

keyIdea.text: Normal and height maps fake geometry detail for lighting, and AO darkens crevices to suggest contact shadows.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Normal · Height · AO
Definition

Normal maps, Height maps, Ambient Occlusion

Techniques for perceived surface detail and localized darkening without extra geometry.

Normal maps
Encode normal perturbation per texel to change how light interacts with the surface.
Height maps
Describe depth for parallax or displacement effects to suggest larger depth variation.
Ambient Occlusion
Multiplies ambient lighting to darken nooks and crevices, reinforcing depth perception.
Example
Barrel planks: normals for fine grain and ridges, subtle height for warped boards, AO in seams for depth.
Import note
Always import normal maps as normal map type to ensure correct interpretation by the shader.
Key Takeaway

Use normal and height maps to fake depth and AO to enhance perceived contact shadows while keeping geometry light.

Troubleshooting
Flat normal symptoms
If shading looks flat, confirm normal map import settings and that the shader reads the normal map slot.
AO misuse
AO should not be used to fake large shadow shapes; it is for local, subtle darkening of crevices.

screens.title: Emission and lighting interaction
screens.narratorSegment: Emission is a material property that makes a surface appear to emit light. Enabling Emission gives the material a self-illuminated color that is added to the shader’s final output. This is useful for screens, light sources, or magical effects where the surface must appear bright regardless of scene lighting. A practical example: on a sphere, checking Emission and increasing its intensity makes it visibly glow even in shadowed areas. Important nuance: emission adds brightness to the rendered pixel but does not necessarily add real light to the scene unless additional systems such as emissive global illumination or light probes are used. In other words, emission affects how the object looks, not automatically how it lights nearby surfaces, unless you enable and bake emissive lighting features. A common misconception is to assume that emission will act like a scene light without further setup. Key takeaway: use Emission for visual glow and pair it with lighting features when you need emissive surfaces to contribute to scene illumination. Emission and lighting interaction means emission makes a surface glow visually; it does not automatically contribute indirect lighting without additional systems enabled.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Core Concept

Emission and lighting interaction

How to make surfaces glow and when that glow affects scene illumination.

Visual emission
Adds a self-illuminated color to the final pixel output, useful for lit screens or magic effects.
Lighting contribution

Example
Make a sphere emit red at high intensity to simulate a glowing orb; note it appears bright even in shadowed parts of the scene.
Misconception

screens.title: Rendering Mode and Transparency
screens.narratorSegment: The Standard Shader exposes a Rendering Mode that controls how the material handles transparency and blending. Typical modes include Opaque, Cutout, Fade, and Transparent. Opaque is the default and is the most performance-friendly because it writes to the depth buffer and avoids costly sorting. Cutout uses an alpha threshold to discard pixels below a cutoff, which is useful for foliage or fences where crisp silhouettes are needed. Fade and Transparent enable smooth alpha blending, but at a higher performance cost and with sorting complications for overlapping transparent surfaces. For instance, using Transparent for many UI or particle elements is appropriate, but applying Transparent to many game-world objects can create overdraw and sorting artifacts. A common mistake is selecting Transparent when Cutout would suffice, leading to unnecessary blending overhead. Another pitfall is relying on alpha-tested Albedo textures with Opaque mode; ensure the chosen mode matches the intended visual and performance characteristics. Key takeaway: choose the rendering mode with both visual needs and runtime performance in mind. Rendering Mode and Transparency means opaque, cutout, fade, transparent each trade off visual blending and performance. match the mode to the visual need.. Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Rendering Mode & Transparency
Definition

Rendering Mode and Transparency

How the Standard Shader blends pixels and the trade-offs for performance and sorting.

Opaque
Fastest path; writes depth, no alpha blending. Use when surface is solid.
Cutout
Alpha-tested silhouette. Good for leaves or grills with sharp edges.
Fade / Transparent
Smooth blending for glass or UI, but incurs sorting and overdraw costs.
Key Takeaway

Select a rendering mode that fits the silhouette and performance needs of your asset. Avoid Transparent unless necessary.

Practical notes
Sorting artifacts
Transparent surfaces can overlap incorrectly. Plan draw order or minimize overlapping transparency to prevent issues.
Performance
Alpha blending increases overdraw. Cutout is cheaper than Fade/Transparent for many masked shapes.

screens.title: Practical walkthrough: Weathered barrel
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough shows how to compose multiple maps to make a weathered wooden barrel look believable. Start by creating a new material using the Standard Shader and assign a high-quality Albedo map showing wood grain and color variation. Next, add a Normal map to simulate plank ridges and small nicks; verify the normal map import setting so it is interpreted correctly by the shader. Then, use a Smoothness map to indicate polished areas—edges worn by use can be slightly higher in smoothness, while dirty or rusted spots are lower. If the barrel has metal bands, use a Metallic map to mark those regions as metal; those areas should also have higher smoothness for polished metal highlights, or lower for rust. Add an Ambient Occlusion map to darken seams and the inside gaps between planks. Finally, tweak Emission only if part of the barrel needs to glow. A concrete example sequence: Albedo with grain → Normal for ridges → AO for seams → Metallic map for bands → Smoothness map for wear. Misconception check: do not bake lighting into Albedo; if shadows are baked into Albedo the material will look wrong under different scene lights. Key takeaway: assemble maps in a deliberate order and preview under varied lighting to ensure consistent realism.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Barrel Walkthrough
Process Flow

Practical walkthrough: Weathered barrel

A stepwise sequence to combine maps and sliders for a believable worn barrel.

  1. Albedo: assign wood grain and color variation. Avoid baked shadows.
  2. Normal: add micro-detail like plank ridges and nicks; ensure normal import is correct.
  3. Ambient Occlusion: darken seams between planks to ground crevices.
  4. Metallic map: mark metal bands as metal; these areas will reflect environment color.
  5. Smoothness map: vary for worn edges versus polished metal; controls reflection sharpness.
  6. Emission (optional): only if parts must glow visually.
Example
Set metal bands Metallic high and Smoothness medium for slightly weathered metal; worn edges show lower Smoothness and altered Albedo.
Check your work
Preview under bright directional light and in indoor, low light scenarios to confirm consistency.
Misconception
Do not bake shadows into Albedo; you will lose correct dynamic shading when lighting changes.
Key Takeaway

Combine maps deliberately, preview under varied lighting, and avoid baking lighting into Albedo for flexible, believable materials.

screens.title: Common mistakes & optimization
screens.narratorSegment: New artists often make predictable mistakes when authoring materials. One is thinking a material equals a single color; color is only one parameter among many that determine an object's character. Another is mixing non-PBR textures with a PBR shader—this mismatch creates implausible responses, especially for metallic and smoothness behavior. Import settings are another frequent source of error: normal maps must be imported as normal type and compression can damage fine detail. On the optimization side, PBR is flexible but can be costly: very high-resolution textures or too many unique materials across many objects increase memory and draw cost. Practical strategies include atlasing textures where possible, using lower-resolution mipmaps for distant objects, and sharing materials across assets when the visual difference is minimal. Also prefer Cutout over Transparent when you need crisp silhouettes, because cutout avoids expensive blending. Concrete scenario: if an open-world scene uses unique 4K textures per prop, memory quickly balloons; instead, target appropriate resolutions per LOD and share maps across similar assets. Key takeaway: verify texture authoring and imports for PBR compatibility and make deliberate compromises to meet platform performance targets.

Comparison

Common mistakes and optimizations

Recognize common pitfalls and apply practical strategies to keep visuals and performance balanced.

Common mistakes
  • Treating material as only color.
  • Using non-PBR textures with PBR shaders.
  • Importing normals incorrectly.
  • Unnecessary Transparent mode causing overdraw.
Optimization strategies
  • Share materials across similar assets.
  • Use appropriate texture resolutions and mipmaps.
  • Atlas textures when feasible.
  • Prefer Cutout to Transparent where valid.
Scenario
Large open-world use of many unique 4K textures will increase memory pressure; target LODs and shared maps to stay within platform limits.
Misconception
Believing PBR alone eliminates the need to optimize textures and material counts is incorrect; PBR improves realism but still requires performance planning.
Key Takeaway

Check texture authoring for PBR compatibility and make pragmatic choices about resolution, atlasing, and material reuse to meet performance targets.

screens.title: Key Concepts

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you will see how materials and shaders together produce the look of every visible object in Unity. Think of a material as the recipe that lists color, texture maps, smoothness, and metallic values. A shader is the chef: it reads the recipe, uses scene lighting and camera position, and performs the math on the graphics hardware to produce the final pixel color you see on screen. We will ground this idea in Physically Based Rendering, the modern approach Unity’s Standard Shader uses to make surfaces react plausibly under any lighting. You’ll learn what Albedo, Metallic, Smoothness, Normal maps, Ambient Occlusion, and Emission do, and you’ll see a practical example of a weathered wooden barrel that combines multiple maps to look realistic. Along the way we’ll highlight common mistakes artists make—like treating a material as only a flat color or mixing non-PBR textures with PBR shaders—and cover performance considerations when authoring materials for target hardware. By the end you should be able to explain the relationship between a material and shader, adjust Standard Shader properties with intent, and identify when a texture needs to be authored in a PBR workflow.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to distinguish materials from shaders, explain how they work together, and apply PBR principles to create consistent, realistic surfaces. You will learn the Standard Shader properties—Albedo, Metallic, Smoothness, Normal, Occlusion, and Emission—and why each matters for the final rendered look. You will practice adjusting these parameters and authoring compatible PBR textures so your assets behave predictably under different lighting conditions. You will also learn to recognize common mistakes, such as treating a material as only a color or mixing non-PBR textures with PBR workflows, and how to avoid performance traps when targeting constrained hardware. Finally, you will complete a hands-on sphere experiment and a weathered barrel walkthrough that will reinforce practical decision-making for real projects. These objectives focus on skills you can verify at milestone checkpoints as you iterate on materials in Unity.

This second objectives slide breaks down the hands-on tasks you will perform and why they matter. You will create a sphere and a new material, then iteratively adjust Albedo, Metallic, and Smoothness to see how each slider influences reflections and color. You will assign Normal and Ambient Occlusion maps to understand how surface detail and self-shadowing add depth without more geometry. You will toggle Emission to learn how a material can appear to glow independently of scene lights. Each task emphasizes observation under different lighting conditions so you can predict how a material will behave in production. These exercises are practical: they build mental models you will reuse when authoring props, characters, or environments. The verified milestones require you to explain observed changes and justify texture authoring decisions, which reinforces transfer from guided practice to real projects.

A material in Unity is a data asset that lists the visual properties of a surface: base color, texture maps, metallic and smoothness values, normal and occlusion maps, and emission settings. It is a collection of values and references to images that describe how the surface should look. A shader is a small program that runs on the graphics hardware and performs per-pixel calculations to combine material properties with lighting and camera information to produce the final visible color. To understand their relationship, imagine making a cake: the material is the recipe listing ingredients and proportions, while the shader is the chef that mixes, heats, and presents the cake. This distinction matters because you can have many materials that use the same shader but with different values; conversely, a shader can be swapped to change how values are interpreted. A common misconception is to call a material a shader. That blurs duties: a material has no execution logic, and a shader without material values has nothing to compute. Example: two plastic toys can share the Standard Shader but differ in Albedo and Smoothness. Misconception check: if a surface appears flat even with a material assigned, verify the shader supports the maps you're using and that your textures were authored for PBR. Key takeaway: treat the material as data and the shader as the program that interprets it.

Physically Based Rendering, or PBR, is a methodology for describing how surfaces interact with light using physically motivated properties. Instead of artist-only tricks for each lighting condition, PBR defines a set of parameters—such as Albedo, Metallic, and Smoothness—that correspond to real-world surface qualities. When you author materials in a PBR workflow, the same material will respond predictably under bright sun, indoor lighting, or colored light sources. That predictability is the main advantage: artists can rely on physical intuition. Concrete example: a metal sphere and a painted plastic sphere with identical Albedo will behave differently if their Metallic and Smoothness values are set correctly; metal will reflect the environment and carry tint, while plastic will scatter light more and show weaker environment reflections. A common misconception is that PBR guarantees photographic realism by default; it does not. PBR guarantees consistent behavior given correct inputs. If textures are authored in a non-PBR pipeline, or metallic maps are incorrect, results will be implausible. Key takeaway: PBR links artist-controlled, physically meaningful parameters to shader calculations so materials remain consistent across scenes and lighting setups.

The Standard Shader in Unity implements a PBR-based rendering model and exposes the key parameters artists use to describe surfaces. At a high level, the shader receives material inputs—Albedo, Metallic, Smoothness, Normal map, Ambient Occlusion, and Emission—and the scene lighting and camera vectors. It first uses Albedo and Metallic to determine diffuse and specular contribution, then applies Smoothness to shape the reflection lobe. Normal maps perturb surface normals so lighting responds to fine detail. Ambient Occlusion multiplies base lighting in crevices to deepen shadows. Emission adds self-illumination that appears to glow regardless of direct lights. A concrete example: the shader may sample Albedo and Metallic maps, compute a fresnel-weighted specular term, blur or sharpen that specular with Smoothness, add normal-based lighting variations, and finally add emission on top. A common misconception is that each slider acts independently; in reality the shader combines them in a formula, so Metallic and Smoothness together determine the character of reflections. Key takeaway: learning how each input participates in the shader’s math helps you predict how changes will appear in scene lighting. Standard Shader overview means standard shader samples material maps, computes diffuse and specular contributions, applies normal perturbation and ao, and adds emission to produce final color.. In practical terms, how the standard shader maps pbr parameters to final pixels. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Albedo, Normal, and Ambient Occlusion maps are fundamental texture inputs for PBR materials. Albedo is the base color map that represents diffuse reflectance; it should not contain baked lighting or shadows because the shader expects neutral base color data. A Normal map encodes surface normals to simulate small-scale bumps and detail without extra geometry; it directly affects how light shades a surface, changing highlight placement and silhouette shading. Ambient Occlusion is a multiplier that darkens crevices and areas less exposed to ambient light, enhancing perceived depth. A concrete example: on a wooden barrel, the Albedo would carry the wood grain and color variations, the Normal map would simulate carved plank ridges, and the AO map would darken crevices between planks. Common mistakes include authoring Albedo with strong shadowing baked in, which reduces the shader's ability to respond correctly to scene lighting, or using a diffuse-styled texture meant for non-PBR pipelines. Another pitfall is forgetting to import normal maps with the correct compression or normal map type, which yields flat or incorrect shading. Key takeaway: author textures for PBR—clean Albedo, proper normal map, and AO for subtle self-shadowing—so the shader can combine them correctly.

Metallic and Smoothness are two of the most impactful properties in the Standard Shader. Metallic controls whether a surface behaves like a conductor—metal—or a dielectric such as plastic or wood. High Metallic causes reflections to carry the surface tint and favor specular energy, while low Metallic leaves color primarily in the diffuse channel. Smoothness controls the microfacet distribution of the surface: high Smoothness produces tight, mirror-like highlights and clear reflections; low Smoothness scatters reflected light, producing a rougher appearance. Together they define the character of reflections. For example, a polished chrome surface will have high Metallic and high Smoothness, making bright, colored reflections; a rough painted metal may have high Metallic but low Smoothness, producing dim and blurred reflections. A common misconception is to treat Smoothness as merely an aesthetic slider; it is a physical parameter that alters light distribution mathematically in the shader. Practical advice: use texture maps for these properties when surfaces vary across the model—like worn edges where metallic paint is scraped away—so the shader computes realistic mixed areas at render time. Key takeaway: adjust Metallic and Smoothness together to model the physical nature of the surface, not to simply make something "shinier."

Normal maps, height maps, and Ambient Occlusion are tools to add surface richness without increasing polygon count. A normal map encodes altered surface normals at the texel level so lighting calculations react as if the surface had micro-geometry. This creates convincing bumps, scratches, or carved details. Height maps (or parallax maps when used) can simulate larger depth shifts by offsetting UVs during shading; they add perceived depth beyond what normal maps provide but can be more expensive. Ambient Occlusion is a grayscale map multiplied into shading to darken crevices where ambient light would be occluded. A practical example: a wooden barrel uses a normal map for plank ridges, a subtle height map to suggest warped planks, and an AO map to deepen the seams between boards. Be careful: importing normal maps properly (flagging them as normal map type) is essential; otherwise the renderer treats them as color textures and shading will be wrong. Misconception check: AO is not a substitute for global illumination; it is a local multiplier to enrich perceived contact shadows. Key takeaway: combine normal, height, and AO maps to increase realism while keeping the base mesh efficient.

Start by creating a new material using the Standard Shader and assign a high-quality Albedo map showing wood grain and color variation. Next, add a Normal map to simulate plank ridges and small nicks; verify the normal map import setting so it is interpreted correctly by the shader. Then, use a Smoothness map to indicate polished areas—edges worn by use can be slightly higher in smoothness, while dirty or rusted spots are lower. If the barrel has metal bands, use a Metallic map to mark those regions as metal; those areas should also have higher smoothness for polished metal highlights, or lower for rust. Add an Ambient Occlusion map to darken seams and the inside gaps between planks. Finally, tweak Emission only if part of the barrel needs to glow. A concrete example sequence: Albedo with grain → Normal for ridges → AO for seams → Metallic map for bands → Smoothness map for wear. Misconception check: do not bake lighting into Albedo; if shadows are baked into Albedo the material will look wrong under different scene lights. Key takeaway: assemble maps in a deliberate order and preview under varied lighting to ensure consistent realism.

New artists often make predictable mistakes when authoring materials. One is thinking a material equals a single color; color is only one parameter among many that determine an object's character. Another is mixing non-PBR textures with a PBR shader—this mismatch creates implausible responses, especially for metallic and smoothness behavior. Import settings are another frequent source of error: normal maps must be imported as normal type and compression can damage fine detail. On the optimization side, PBR is flexible but can be costly: very high-resolution textures or too many unique materials across many objects increase memory and draw cost. Practical strategies include atlasing textures where possible, using lower-resolution mipmaps for distant objects, and sharing materials across assets when the visual difference is minimal. Also prefer Cutout over Transparent when you need crisp silhouettes, because cutout avoids expensive blending. Concrete scenario: if an open-world scene uses unique 4K textures per prop, memory quickly balloons; instead, target appropriate resolutions per LOD and share maps across similar assets. Key takeaway: verify texture authoring and imports for PBR compatibility and make deliberate compromises to meet platform performance targets.

Here are the essential concepts to carry forward. First, a Material is a data asset that defines a surface by storing maps and numeric parameters; a Shader is the program that uses that data with lighting to render pixels. Second, PBR is the workflow that ties physical surface properties like Albedo, Metallic, and Smoothness to consistent visual responses under differing lighting. Third, author textures for PBR: keep Albedo free of baked lighting, import Normal maps correctly, and use AO for subtle crevice shadows. Keep these three points in mind as quick checks when authoring materials: data versus program, PBR parameters for physical behavior, and correct texture authoring. Ask yourself at each step whether textures are PBR-ready and whether the chosen shader supports the intended maps. This habit will save time and prevent common visual errors.
